extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers studying American government, constitutional law, and the federal judiciary
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter overviewing the structure, powers, jurisdiction, officers, and procedural principles of the United States federal judiciary, aimed at explaining why the federal courts were established and how they operate. Includes descriptions of court classes, tenure, jurisdictional categories, removal rules, and relationships with State courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for establishing federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: National tribunals were necessary because under the Confederation there were no means of enforcing treaties or orders of Congress, State courts were ill-fitted for quasi-international matters (admiralty, treaty rights), could not decide questions between States, and might disregard Federal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that federal courts were created to interpret/apply federal laws and compel obedience, to provide a neutral forum for disputes between States or citizens of different States, and to preserve uniformity of decision on subjects within the Constitution's purview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes of Federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal courts fall into four classes: The Supreme Court, The Circuit Courts of Appeals, The Circuit courts, and The District courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that the Constitution drew the outlines of the system and Congress perfected it by statute; details rest on statutes and therefore Congress may alter them. Suggests studying the system for its complexity and smooth working.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court creation, composition, and appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court is directly created by Art. III §1. Originally six justices; at the time of writing nine (a chief justice and eight associates). Justices are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives historical numbers and salaries as context; affirms constitutional origin and appointment process as fundamental features of the Court's composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life tenure and judicial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal judges 'hold office during good behaviour,' i.e., life tenure removable only by impeachment, intended to secure independence of the judiciary from legislative/political pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains Framers' rationale: life tenure is a bulwark against legislative or executive encroachment; impeachment has been rare; Congressional proposals to limit tenure have been rejected; overall tenure has justified expectations of judicial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court sittings and decision procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court sits from October till June; the presence of six judges is required to pronounce a decision; every case is discussed twice—once to ascertain the majority opinion and again to review the written judgment prepared by one judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: requiring a quorum prevents division of the Court into branches and ensures thorough consideration, albeit slowing dispatch of business; description of formal sittings and adoption of written judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit Courts of Appeals structure and operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Circuit Courts of Appeal were created by Congress; there are judicial circuits (nine at time of writing), with two to four Circuit judges per circuit, and one Supreme Court justice allotted to each; panels may sit in various combinations (Circuit judge alone, Supreme Court justice alone, together, with or without District judge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes appeal paths: cases come from District courts to Circuit Courts of Appeal, with further appeal in some cases to the Supreme Court; notes historical abolition of former Circuit courts and transfer of jurisdiction to District courts (1912).

rubrics_metrics.name: District courts details and appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts are the lowest Federal tribunals (eighty-eight in 1910); their judges receive statutory salaries and, though the Constitution does not expressly state the appointment mode for these judges, appointments have been made by the President with Senate confirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States practical arrangements and that Congressional statutes govern the number and details of District courts and judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special federal tribunals (Court of Claims; Court of Customs Appeals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Special tribunals exist for particular classes of disputes: a Court of Claims (for private persons' claims against the Federal government) with a chief justice and justices, and a Court of Customs Appeals (created under the Tariff Act of 1909) to decide customs duty questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes salaries, composition, and that appeals from these courts may lie directly to the Supreme Court; shows Congress can create specialized tribunals by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction: cases arising under the Constitution, laws, and treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: "Cases in law and equity arising under the constitution, the laws of the United States, and treaties made under their authority."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This brings before Federal courts every cause where either party relies on a Federal enactment, entitling plaintiffs to bring actions in Federal court and defendants to remove cases originally in State court when a federal enactment is relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction: cases affecting ambassadors, public ministers, and consuls
rubrics_metrics.description: "Cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: such persons have an international character and it would be improper for State courts (which are local) to deal with them; Federal courts provide the necessary learning and securities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction: admiralty and maritime jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: "Cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction," including prize cases, maritime contracts, and navigation-related transactions (on navigable lakes, rivers, and high seas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why admiralty matters are assigned to Federal courts as inherently national or international in character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction: controversies to which the United States is a party
rubrics_metrics.description: "Controversies to which the United States shall be a party."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessary to protect the United States from being obliged to sue or be sued in a State court whose decisions the national government could not be expected to submit to; pecuniary claims against the Federal government are handled by the Court of Claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction: diversity and interstate/foreign controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: "Controversies between two or more States, between a State and citizens of another State, between citizens of different States, between citizens of the same State claiming lands under grants of different States, and between a State, or the citizens thereof, and foreign States, citizens, or subjects."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: to avoid partial State tribunals and ensure unbiased, competent adjudication which promotes interstate commerce and confidence; notes historical objections leading to the Eleventh Amendment curbing some suits against States by private plaintiffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal rule from State to Federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Judiciary Act (1789) removal is allowed where a federal question (validity of a treaty, statute, or authority) is drawn in question in the State court and the decision is against their validity, or where a State statute's validity is questioned and the decision is in favor of its validity; removal is authorized only if it appears in the record that such a question arose and was passed upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the motive: if a State court applies a federal enactment the supremacy is recognized and no removal is needed; if the State court denies applicability, the aggrieved party has the right to carry the point to the Supreme Court. Also notes procedural details about timing and judgment-stage removals.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts lack power to inquire into federal executive acts (habeas corpus limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: State courts have no jurisdiction to release on habeas corpus or otherwise inquire into the lawfulness of detention by Federal authority when the arrest has been made by a Federal officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Chief Justice Taney's statement that the powers of the general government and of the State are separate sovereignties acting within their respective spheres, so State courts cannot exercise judicial process over Federal action in that sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign immunity and Eleventh Amendment constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: A principal objection to the Constitution was that it might expose a State to be sued by individuals of another State; after Chisholm v. Georgia (1793) an Eleventh Amendment was passed declaring the judicial power shall not extend to suits commenced or prosecuted against one of the United States by citizens of another State or by citizens or subjects of any foreign state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains historical reaction (States' outrage), the amendment's passage, and its practical effect (protection of States, enabling some repudiations of debt), and notes exceptions and interpretations (e.g., applicability to certain kinds of appeals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original vs appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court's jurisdiction is original in cases affecting ambassadors and where a State is a party; in other cases it is appellate; jurisdiction may be exclusive in some matters and concurrent in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes complexity and many difficult questions arising from concurrent jurisdictions; also that State courts cannot be invested by Congress with federal jurisdiction since Congress has no authority over them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal jurisdiction of Federal courts is statutory
rubrics_metrics.description: The criminal jurisdiction of the Federal courts extends only to offences against Federal law and is purely statutory—'The United States as such can have no common law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that federal powers derive from the Constitution and are found in written law; contrasts federal statutory criminal jurisdiction with state common-law traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure prescribed by Congress subject to constitutional safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure in Federal courts is prescribed by Congress, subject to Constitution-preserved rules (e.g., the right to trial by jury in criminal cases and in suits at common law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that because 'cases in law and equity' are mentioned in the Constitution, Congress could not fully fuse law and equity procedures as in some States/England and must maintain the distinct methods of procedure even if administered by the same judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of law and reliance on State court decisions when applying State law
rubrics_metrics.description: When federal law is not applicable (e.g., suits between citizens of different States), the Federal court must determine which State's law governs and then apply that law; in administering State law the Federal courts ought to follow the decisions of the State courts as the highest authority on that State's law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that the Supreme Court has even overruled its own previous determinations on a point of State law to conform with the view of the highest court of the particular State; also that State courts generally follow Federal courts on Federal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal court officers and enforcement machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Federal court has an attached United States marshal responsible for executing writs, judgments, and orders (arrests, levies, possession), and a United States district attorney who prosecutes Federal offences; both are under the direction of the Attorney General.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marshal may call on citizens for help or, failing that, obtain Federal troops for enforcement; together these officials form a network of Federal authorities independent of State officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional control over federal court details via statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: While the Constitution sets the outlines of the Federal judiciary, Congress perfects the system by statute and retains the power to alter details (number of courts, organization, jurisdictional particulars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit standard: many features of the federal judiciary (courts' existence, jurisdictions, procedures, salaries) are statutory and subject to congressional change; examples include creation of Courts of Appeals, special tribunals, and changes in circuit/district organization.
